transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-03
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~54 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Alison Park (LumenPay), Marco Ruiz (LumenPay), Sara Kim (LumenPay)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache with a cost-model overlay. Discussed typical seq lengths for LumenPay, caching hit rates, and what to expect from a pilot.

00:00 Jordan: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood, i'll hand off to Maya in a minute for the technical walkthrough but quick agenda, we'll go through Optimize, batching best practices, prefix vs KV cache, then cost models and next steps
00:18 Maya: hey all, thanks. so first quick clarifying q - what are your typical request types and average token lengths?
00:26 Alison: yeah mostly transaction summarization and compliance chat, median length is pretty short, like 40 to 120 tokens, but we do have longer reconciliation queries up to 800 tokens occasionally
00:40 Marco: also we have bursty traffic at end of day and month end, so throughput matters, and tail latency is a big no-no for our customer UX
00:54 Maya: great, that distribution maps to the batching strategies we'll recommend; small median length favors continuous batching with small windows to keep latency low, but we can still batch opportunistically by route
01:08 Jordan: just to call out, Optimize has a route-level config so you can tune per-endpoint, e.g., chat-vs-embeds or reconciliation-vs-summary
01:22 Alison: curious about prefix cache — we've heard about KV cache too. when do we use one vs the other?
01:30 Maya: good q. prefix cache is great for repeated prompts/boilerplate, it's effectively LRU on token prefixes; KV cache is more explicit for long session state, like chat history where you want to persist the KV and avoid recomputing attention states. both reduce compute but they behave differently for hit rate and memory footprint
01:48 Marco: is KV cache persistent across requests or is it in-memory on the GPU?
01:53 Maya: by default KV cache lives in GPU memory for fastest hits, but with Dedicated or Private you can configure eviction and a hot-tier in RAM; we also support prefix-level serialization for warm starts in our Dedicated offering
02:08 Sara: any ballpark on hit rate improvements we should expect? our prompts are templated but users tweak them a bit
02:14 Maya: templated prompts are good — if you have canonical prefixes you'll see high prefix hit rates, like 40-70% depending on variance; KV cache for session-based chat can push effective compute reduction further because you only process new tokens. we'll model this in the cost spreadsheet
02:32 Jordan: speaking of cost, we prepared three scenarios — hosted API (pay-as-you-go), Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private deployment. the spreadsheet has assumptions for qps, average tokens, batching windows, and cache hit rates
02:44 Jordan: e.g., for your distribution, with a 50% prefix hit and 30% KV hit, hosted is cheapest at low QPS, Dedicated becomes more cost-effective at sustained high throughput, and Private makes sense if you need strict data residency or a specific KMS/HSM integration
03:05 Marco: when you say batching windows, how do you balance latency? we can't accept more than 200ms p95 on summaries
03:12 Maya: two levers — batch timeout and max-batch-size. with median 60 tokens we recommend 15-25ms timeout and dynamic batch sizing. that keeps p50/p95 low while still capturing micro-batches. Optimize suggests per-route defaults and shows expected latencies in the console
03:30 Jordan: a note about tail latency: we do background pre-warm for long-running request patterns and model fallback to smaller model variants when under memory pressure to keep tail SLOs
03:46 Alison: ok that's helpful. can you run through the cost model numbers quickly? rough order of magnitude is fine now
03:52 Jordan: sure — so quick example from the spreadsheet: assume 100 qps, avg 80 tokens, batch settings as above, and cache hit 50% prefix + 25% KV. Hosted cost per 1M tokens = $X (placeholder in demo) but real spreadsheet will give line items — model compute, GPU seconds, storage for KV, and network. Dedicated amortizes GPU-hour cost across throughput so per-token drops ~30-45% at sustained loads in our model
04:22 Maya: also important: KV cache storage can add fixed storage and retrieval costs if you persist to hot-tier, so we model both memory-only and memory+ram persistence scenarios in the sheet
04:40 Marco: latency impact for KV retrieval? does rehydration add latency spikes?
04:45 Maya: short answer: usually negligible if hot in GPU memory. if it spills to RAM or SSD there's an extra 5-50ms depending on tier. Optimize highlights that and will flag routes likely to spill given your session sizes
05:02 Sara: on security side we need SOC2 + KMS integration, and logs for audits, also SSO and RBAC for redwood console access
05:12 Jordan: yep we have SOC2 docs — i'll share — and we integrate with customer KMS for Private or Dedicated, hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default but can support CMKs on enterprise plans; console has SAML SSO and RBAC roles
05:30 Alison: any gotchas we should plan for during a pilot? thinking about test data, obfuscation, and latency measurement accuracy
05:40 Maya: for pilots we recommend a replay harness using production request traces (anonymized). we'll run the benchmark both on your sample data and our synthetic load to validate batching behavior. measure token-level cost and p50/p95 latencies, and we'll compare hosted vs Dedicated estimates
06:02 Jordan: one more thing — model variant fallbacks: Optimize can automatically route to a smaller/cheaper variant when load spikes or if it detects QoS issues. that helps control costs without manual rollbacks
06:18 Marco: do you support quantized variants in Dedicated? we want to test int8 to save costs
06:23 Maya: yes Dedicated supports quantized kernels and we show perf/quality tradeoffs. the cost model includes quality-adjusted effective throughput if you enable quantization
06:35 Alison: ok, i'd like to see a concrete run with our data and the cost spreadsheet filled in. also want to ensure the KV cache keying scheme fits our tenant model (multi-tenant routing)
06:48 Maya: keying is per-tenant; we recommend namespacing keys and we can show the sample config. also, Optimize console visualizes cache hit rates per-tenant so you can monitor regressions
07:02 Jordan: quick demo — screen share — slides open — (demo noise)
07:10 Maya: here is the Optimize console, route config panel, batching slider, and cache toggles. you can change batch timeout and immediately see estimated p95 impact and per-token cost delta
07:32 Maya: example: increasing batch timeout from 10ms to 25ms increases throughput and lowers per-token compute by ~18% but p95 goes from 120ms to ~190ms in this scenario
07:48 Alison: if we have mixed routes, can you do different defaults per route?
07:52 Maya: yep route defaults plus inheritance. you can set org-level policies too so platform teams can lock certain behaviors for production routes
08:06 Marco: about telemetry — how granular are the cost breakdowns? we need token-level, per-model, per-route cost attribution for chargeback
08:14 Jordan: console gives token-level breakdown by model+route+token-type (prompt/completion); you can export CSV and connect to our cost API for automated billing attribution
08:30 Sara: any previous customers in payments/fintech you can reference? we need references for compliance review
08:36 Jordan: yes — we've worked with Aurora Finance and NovaBank on Dedicated pilots; i'll include reference contacts in the follow-up email
08:48 Alison: ok perfect. couple follow-ups — one, can you include estimated memory footprint for KV per active session? two, we want to know how cache invalidation would work across releases
08:58 Maya: we'll add a per-session KV footprint table in the spreadsheet — and for invalidation we support TTLs, versioned keys, and orchestrated invalidations via API so you can flush per-tenant during deploys
09:18 Marco: curious about cost breakdown: network egress between regions if we do private in country? we have EU data residency needs
09:26 Jordan: for Private we can deploy in EU region and set data residency; network egress charges depend on customer infra but our model will include region-specific bandwidth costs as a line item
09:38 Alison: also, how fast can we spin up a Dedicated pool for a pilot if we go down that road?
09:45 Jordan: typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for reserved pools, we can provision a small pilot quicker using burst capacity on hosted while we provision Dedicated if that helps your timeline
09:58 Sara: timeline-wise we want a pilot before EOY, ideally mid-december results — is that feasible?
10:06 Jordan: yes if we kick off the benchmark this month and you provide sample traces we'll aim for mid-Dec results; next steps in the sheet reflect that
10:18 Alison: any assumptions in the model about prompt engineering changes? we may change prompts to be more concise which will affect tokens
10:24 Maya: we include sensitivity scenarios for token reduction (10-30% fewer tokens) to show cost delta — we'll run one with your likely prompt compressions and one baseline
10:35 Marco: slight tangent — are there throttles or hard limits we should be aware of on hosted? we need guaranteed throughput during payroll runs
10:42 Jordan: hosted is shared, so we recommend Dedicated for guaranteed throughput and SLAs; hosted has quotas and burst policies but no firm capacity commits unless you buy a Dedicated contract
10:56 Alison: ok that aligns with our thinking. let's talk about pilot success criteria — low cost per 1M tokens, p95 under 200ms on summary routes, and KV hit >30%
11:08 Jordan: agreed. we'll put those success criteria in the pilot charter and include them in the follow-up email
11:20 Maya: any other technical questions?
11:23 Marco: one more — how do you measure cache hit skew across tenants? if a few tenants dominate hits does that reduce others' benefits?
11:33 Maya: yes that's a real pattern; Optimize reports per-tenant hit rates and suggests per-tenant cache partitioning or sizing. for Dedicated you can reserve memory per-tenant if needed
11:45 Alison: thanks, that's great.
11:48 Jordan: cool, quick recap of next steps: i'll send the spreadsheet, SOC2 and references; Maya will own benchmarks; Marco will send traces; Sara will confirm security stakeholders. we'll target a benchmark run week of 2026-11-09 and follow up mid-December with results
12:10 Alison: thanks everyone, appreciate it
12:14 Jordan: thanks all, talk soon
